title: Christmas Week
body: The Week arrives as it does every December: the races, the gymkhana, the amateur theatricals in which the Judge is once again the villain, and the Club ball for which the ice has been coming down by rail in sawdust since Tuesday. Parcels from Home are opened a month stale and read twice. For six days the station contrives, by united effort, to believe itself eleven thousand miles from where it is. No business of any kind is transacted, and the district, which has seen many Christmases, waits politely for the sahibs to finish.
outcome: It is absurd, and touching, and over by Twelfth Night. The files have not moved; the district has kept itself; and every man in the station is, for a week at least, easier to live with — including you.

title: The Commissioner's Cold-Weather Inspection
body: The Commissioner comes through in February, as he comes through every February: forty tents, a red carpet that travels in its own cart, and a notebook whose pencilled entries have ended better careers than yours. He will see the jail, the schools, the treasury, and whatever else is put in front of him, and he will form — over three days and two dinners — the single sentence about you that Simla will read.

choices.label: Paint the district for him — whitewash, garlands, and the contented poor at intervals.
choices.outcome: The jail is limewashed, the school recites, and a line of the reliably contented is arranged at the roadside with garlands. The Commissioner, who has inspected districts for thirty years and believes none of what he is shown, is nonetheless soothed by the effort of the deception, which is the real tribute. The sentence, this year, is a good one.

choices.label: Show him the district as it is and let the work speak.

ifTrue.outcome: You show him the unwhitewashed jail, the honest arrears, the things half-done and the reasons why. It is a gamble on the man having once been a district officer himself — and it comes off: he grunts, corrects your canal figures from memory, and writes the word ‘sound,’ which from him is a garland.

ifFalse.outcome: Honesty is a fine policy for a district that will bear looking at, and yours, just now, will not. The pencil moves in the notebook at the jail, at the school, at the third unmended culvert; and the sentence Simla reads this year has the word ‘slack’ in it, which takes precisely one cold weather to earn and three to live down.

choices.label: Give him a durbar to remember — the whole district by rank on the maidan.
choices.outcome: A shamiana like a landed cloud, the notables seated to the inch of their precedence, the schoolchildren massed, the police burnished. The Commissioner is received like a minor king and departs purring; the cost is entered under four different heads, none of them called what it was; and the district notes what its magistrate will spend on a carpet who pleaded poverty at the last assessment.

title: Empire Day
body: The twenty-fourth of May, and the thermometer at a hundred and eleven. The schools are drawn up on the maidan by eight, the flag hangs like a dead thing on its staff, the loyal address is seventeen minutes long, and the Municipal Committee to a man is wearing broadcloth. Somewhere at the back a child has already fainted. The Empire, which does not feel the heat, expects to be honoured at full length; the assembled district, which does, watches to see how much of the sun the sahib will take.

choices.label: Take the whole parade at attention, address and all.
choices.outcome: You stand through every verse of it, bareheaded for the anthem with the sun like a hand on your skull, and take the salute as though the maidan were the Horse Guards. The district approves of the performance in the way it approves of any penance properly done. That evening your head rings like a struck gong, and the Civil Surgeon uses the word ‘folly’ conversationally.

choices.label: Cut it mercifully short and get the children into the shade.
choices.outcome: You take the address as read, decorate the head boy, and have the schools dismissed to the trees and the water-carriers by half-past eight. The mothers of the district are with you to a woman; the Municipal Committee, robbed of its seventeen minutes, is not; and the Colonel observes at the Club that in his day Empire Day was Empire Day.

choices.label: Let Mukherjee take the salute; you are indisposed.
choices.outcome: The Deputy Collector takes the parade faultlessly — rather better, in fact, than you would have done, which is noted on all sides with varying satisfaction. You spend the morning behind the chiks with the returns. The precedent, once set, will be remembered by everyone: by the district with interest, and by the Club with the particular silence it keeps for a sahib who was not there.

title: The Birthday Gazette
body: The June list is out for the King-Emperor's birthday, and the Gazette is passed down the Club table with the soda. A Commissioner you have met twice is advanced to Knight Commander; a Political no one can place gets his C.I.E. for a treaty everyone calls a picnic; the Colonel's brother-in-law is remembered at last. Your name is not in it. There was no reason it should be — the year is not done and the list was made in March — and you read it twice all the same, and put it down with particular carelessness.
outcome: The soda goes round again. Somebody says ‘next year, perhaps,’ without looking at anyone, and the conversation moves gratefully on to the state of the polo ponies. The Gazette lies on the table the rest of the evening, face up, like something at an inquest.

title: The Breach in the Bund
body: The wire comes up from Kasauli ghat at two in the morning, which is the hour such wires keep: the great bund is going. Forty years of flood have leaned on it and this is the year it means to win — a hundred yards of embankment weeping brown water, and below it, in the dark, thirty villages and the winter rice of half a tehsil. The engineer gives it a week. Lala Hukum Chand, who can produce coolies, brick, and boats faster than Government can produce a sanction, has already — with his compliments and his terms — sent a man to ask whether the Collector-sahib will be wanting anything.

choices.label: Take the Lala's money and rebuild the bund at once, terms be damned.
choices.outcome: By dawn there are nine hundred men on the embankment and the Lala's brick coming down by the boatload, and in six days of mud and lanterns the bund is a bund again. The villages are saved and know who saved them. The terms, when you read them at leisure, are the terms of a man who also knows — and who has waited years for the river to deliver you to his book.

choices.label: Patch the worst of it from the treasury and stand the watch yourself.
choices.outcome: You spend what the chest will bear, press every Public Works man and district cart into the breach, and take the night watches in a streaming mackintosh with the water a foot from the lip. The bund holds — barely, this year. The engineer's report calls the repair ‘temporary,’ which is what the district calls everything Government does, and the treasury will feel it at settlement.

choices.label: The bund has held forty years; hold the money and trust the odds.
choices.outcome: The river, which has also been playing the odds for forty years, calls. The breach goes out on the ninth night with a sound the district will describe for a generation, and the water takes the rice, the cattle, and eleven lives the enquiry will call ‘regrettably unavoidable.’ It also takes — quietly, completely — the district’s belief that the sahib stands between it and the river, which was most of what the sahib had.

title: The Fever Week
body: August, and the district's fever season arrives on the schedule it has kept since before the Company. The tanks are green, the air is a wet blanket, and the mosquitoes hold the low ground in force. Half the office is absent or shivering at its desk; the jail hospital is full; the quinine goes round the bungalow table with the salt. You take your five grains a day, feel the first familiar ache behind the eyes on Thursday, and go on with the files, because the alternative is also the fever, with the files unread.
outcome: It is nobody's fault and nothing to be done: it is the country itself, presenting its annual account. By the month's end the office refills, a little yellower; the returns are made up late and no one in Simla asks why; and the ache retreats to wherever it winters, keeping your address.

title: The Annual Administration Report
body: October, and the year must now be turned into prose. The Annual Administration Report goes up through the Commissioner to Government, and it is the one document in which a district may be anything its magistrate has the nerve to call it: the figures are appendices, but the sentences are yours. Ram Autar lays the draft materials on the desk in perfect order and withdraws to a tactful distance, and the whole twelvemonth — the tours and the fevers and the files — waits to hear what officially happened.

choices.label: Varnish it — a year of steady progress under review.

ifTrue.outcome: The prose glows, and the figures — decent enough, this year, to bear it — do not contradict a word. Government reads of firm and sympathetic administration, notes the collections, and is satisfied. It is not exactly untrue, which is the whole art of the Annual Report; and only you and Ram Autar know which adjectives are load-bearing.

ifFalse.outcome: The prose glows; the appendices do not. A Deputy Secretary with a taste for arithmetic sets the adjectives against the arrears and minutes, frostily, that the Collector’s satisfaction with his district appears to rest on grounds not disclosed in the tables. A varnished report over bad figures is the one lie the Service never forgives, because it makes the reader do the work.

choices.label: Write it plainly — the year as it actually went.
choices.outcome: You set down the failures with the successes, and the reasons for both, in prose with no varnish in it. Government finds the document ‘candid,’ which in the official lexicon sits two shelves below ‘brilliant’; but it is a report a man can stand behind at an enquiry, and you sleep the sounder for every plain sentence in it.

choices.label: Let Ram Autar draft it in the full ceremonial style.
choices.outcome: The head clerk composes forty pages of faultless official prose in which nothing is concealed and nothing can quite be found — grievances dissolved in the passive voice, arrears distributed among subordinate clauses. Government reads it with the mild pleasure of recognition, for half the province’s reports are written by such men in such a style. You sign it. It is, in every sense, the district’s own account of itself.
